reason: The sources provide 15 distinct claims supported by at least two sites regarding the overpressure anomaly and the secret spy satellite mission.
story: The 1981 launch of Space Shuttle Columbia was the boldest test in history, marking the first time NASA launched a new crewed ship without an uncrewed trial. But at ignition, an unexpected overpressure wave from the solid rocket boosters slammed into the orbiter. The force was so violent it ripped 16 thermal tiles off and damaged 148 more. Fearing the ship might disintegrate during reentry, NASA officials turned to the shadows. In a secret operation known as 'The Plan,' they coordinated with the National Reconnaissance Office to use a Top Secret KH-11 spy satellite. Controllers even adjusted the launch timing to ensure the 'black bird' could photograph Columbia's belly. While the crew glimpsed the secret satellite from their windows, the top-secret images confirmed the damage was not fatal. Columbia landed safely at Edwards Air Force Base, but the near-miss forced a complete redesign of launchpad sound suppression.
angle: NASA had to use a Top Secret spy satellite to check if the first Space Shuttle was falling apart in orbit after a launch shockwave ripped off its heat shield.

claims.claim: STS-1 was the first orbital flight of NASA's Space Shuttle program.
The crew consisted of Commander John Young and Pilot Robert Crippen.
It was the first time solid-fuel rockets were used for a NASA crewed launch.
STS-1 was the first US crewed space vehicle launched without a prior uncrewed powered test flight.
An overpressure wave occurred upon ignition of the solid rocket boosters.
The overpressure wave caused the loss of 16 thermal protection tiles.
The overpressure wave damaged 148 tiles in addition to those lost.
NASA used a secret KH-11 reconnaissance satellite, also known as Kennen, to photograph the orbiter's tiles.
The launch time was specifically chosen or adjusted to coordinate with the spy satellite's orbit.
The KH-11 spy satellite experienced a major attitude control problem shortly before the shuttle launch.
The shuttle crew glimpsed the KH-11 spy satellite from orbit.
Columbia landed on Runway 23 at Edwards Air Force Base in California.
The mission coincided with the 20th anniversary of Yuri Gagarin's first spaceflight.
Columbia spent 610 days in the Orbiter Processing Facility before its maiden launch.

disputed: The specific claim that the body flap was pushed to an angle where hydraulic rupture was expected is only detailed in [S1]; the script should attribute this to mission anomaly reports.
NASA's public reason for the launch delay was a computer reboot, but [S3] and [S5] dispute this, stating it was for satellite alignment; attribute the reboot as the 'official cover story.'
John Young's claim about hot gas buckling the landing gear door is noted as missing from some versions of official reports; the script should handle this as a post-flight discovery by the Commander.
